identifier: Frank E. Jones and Georgia L. Harris, "ITS-90 Density of Water Formulation for Volumetric Standards Calibration", Journal of Research of the National Institute of Standards and Technology 97, 335-340 (Volume 97, Number 3, May-June 1992), accepted 27 April 1992. The value entered is the 20.0 degC cell of Table 1, the 0.0 tenths column: density of AIR-SATURATED water in g/cm^3 from equation 6 using Kell's data.
grade_rule: E3, grade_tag peer_reviewed. Another laboratory's published result: 10.3 rule 1's 'a run elsewhere is not a run here' caps it at E3 however carefully it was made. Within E3 the sort ranks peer_reviewed above vendor_spec.
license_note: United States government work, public domain. Numeric table values and stated conditions only. No text, figure or equation is reproduced into an entry.
method_as_stated: Not a measurement paper. It presents a new formulation of the density of air-saturated water as a function of temperature on ITS-90, for the range 5 to 40 degC, intended for the gravimetric determination of the volume of volumetric standards. Table 1 tabulates equation 6 at 0.1 degC steps; Table 2 tabulates air-free water from equation 3; Table 3 reproduces the older Wagenbreth and Blanke formulation for comparison.
how_the_tabulated_value_was_produced: A FORMULATION FITTED TO KELL'S DATA, PUBLISHED IN THIS PAPER AS ITS OWN RESULT. Table 1's caption says so on its face -- 'from Eq. (6) using Kell [2] data' -- so the measurement chain is Kell's and the reduction onto ITS-90 is this paper's. That is the same standing as src_tilton_taylor_1938_water_index's Table 5, which is that paper's least-squares reduction of its own measurements, in the one respect rule 5 cares about: the fit was done by the authors and published in the primary paper, not reproduced by a third party into a database. The difference -- whose measurements were fitted -- is recorded here rather than smoothed over, because it is the reason this is E3 and not something better, and because a reader tracing the number to its origin has two hops to make and not one.
why_this_and_not_the_alternatives: TILTON AND TAYLOR 1937 WAS READ FIRST AND SET ASIDE ON A UNIT. Their RP971, 'Accurate representation of the refractivity and density of distilled water as a function of temperature', J. Res. NBS 18, 205, prints Table 2 -- density of distilled water computed from Chappuis' observations -- and its 20.0 degC cell reads 0.9982336. That table is NOT in g/cm^3: the paper states in its own words that 'the unit of density is 1 g per milliliter', meaning the 1901 millilitre defined as the volume of one gram of water at maximum density, which is why the table prints exactly 1.0000000 at 4 degC. Entering 0.9982336 under the registered unit g/cm^3 would have asserted a value wrong by 2.8e-5 relative, and units.json cannot hold the distinction: it registers g/cm^3 and mg/ml, and its mg/ml treats the millilitre as exactly a cubic centimetre. Converting is a step this store may not take -- it would make the number `computed:` at E4 and would need a second source for the millilitre-to-cubic-centimetre factor. So the 1937 paper is a correct source for a number in a unit this repository cannot express, and this 1992 paper is a correct source for the same physical quantity in a unit it can. IAPWS-95 and the CIPM-2001 formulation (Tanaka et al., Metrologia 38) are formulations rather than printed values, the same objection that kept IAPWS R9-97 out of the refractive-index entry. Huber et al., J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data 38, 21 (2009) is a reference correlation; its srd.nist.gov reprint is the host that returned HTTP 503 during the refractive-index work on 2026-09-20 and was not retried here because this paper already answers at a printed grid point.
the_two_tables_differ_by_air_saturation: Table 1 is air-saturated water and Table 2 is air-free, and at 20.0 degC they read 0.998201 and 0.998203 g/cm^3 -- a difference of 2e-6, which is 2 ppm. The air-saturated table is the one entered, because a sample sitting open on a bench is in contact with the atmosphere. That is a claim about the bench and not about the paper, so it is recorded in the entry's validity_conditions where a caller can disagree with it; the air-free value is a printed cell of the same paper and can be filed as a second entry on request.
cross_checked_against_the_1937_paper: THE TWO SOURCES AGREE TO 2.6e-6 ONCE THE MILLILITRE IS ACCOUNTED FOR, AND THAT IS WHAT CONFIRMS BOTH READINGS. Tilton and Taylor's 0.9982336 g per 1901 millilitre divided by 1.000028 is 0.9982056 g/cm^3, against this paper's air-free 0.998203 -- two measurement chains fifty-five years apart. The check cuts two ways: it confirms the table cells were read off the right rows, and it confirms the unit diagnosis, because taking the 1937 number as g/cm^3 would have disagreed with this paper by 2.8e-5, twenty times worse than the residual. The arithmetic was done only to verify the reading and is not the basis of any entered number; the entered value is a printed cell.
note: READ FROM THE PRINTED TABLE. Table 1 gives whole degrees down the stub and tenths across, and every cell prints all six decimals with no carried leading digits, so the reading hazard that RP1085's Table 5 has is absent here. The 20.0 degC cell is the first column of the row labelled 20, read as 0.998201, with the rows at 19 and 21 reading 0.998402 and 0.997989 in the same column -- monotone decreasing through the row, as it must be above 4 degC.
not_entered: The rest of Table 1 (5 to 40 degC at 0.1 degC steps), all of Table 2 (air-free), all of Table 3 (Wagenbreth and Blanke, printed for comparison), equation 6 and its six constants, and the isothermal compressibility equation. Any cell is a printed value and needs no interpolation as long as the temperature asked for lands on a tabulated argument; the table's step is 0.1 degC throughout, with no change of grid of the kind RP1085's Table 7 has.
caveat: DISTILLED WATER, NOT THE SUSPENSION ON THIS BENCH. particle_suspension_a is not pure water, and using this density for it is a substitution the caller makes and records. The formulation's stated range is 5 to 40 degC and 20 degC sits well inside it. Temperatures are ITS-90 by the paper's whole purpose, so 20.0 degC is 293.15 K with no scale conversion of the kind the 1938 index paper needs.
